lead: A distributed computation is a set of processes, each running its own sequence of events. Events are internal steps, sends and receives. The only link between processes is messages. The model says what we may assume about timing, message delay and failures. Those assumptions decide whether a timeout is a proof or a guess. The same code can be correct on one model and wrong on another. This chapter sets out the synchronous and asynchronous models and the round-based programs that sit between them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for what a distributed system is, and Chapter 4.2 for send and receive.

blocks.text: A process is a program running on one computer. Its local history is the sequence of events it performs. An event is one of three things: an internal step (a local computation), a send of a message, or a receive of a message. A send and its matching receive are two events, one in each process. They are linked by the message, not by a shared clock.

An execution (also called a run) is one complete set of events of all processes plus the messages between them. The events of one process are totally ordered: that process does them one after another. Events of different processes are not automatically ordered. If no message chain connects two events, either order is possible. So an execution is a partial order, not a single sequence. This is why two machines can disagree about which of two events happened first; Chapter 4.6 turns this into logical clocks.

A state-based view treats each process as a state machine. It has a state s and a transition function δ: on an event e it moves to s′ = δ(s, e). A send adds a message to a channel; a receive removes one. The global state is the vector of local states plus the messages in transit. Snapshot algorithms in Chapter 4.8 capture such a global state without stopping the system.

A failure model says what can go wrong. The common ones are crash (a process stops and stays stopped), fail-stop (a crash that other processes can detect), omission (a process fails to send or receive some messages), and Byzantine (a process may behave arbitrarily, including lying). This chapter only names them; Unit 5 develops them.

sections.h3: Synchronous model: bounds you can trust

blocks.text: In the synchronous model every process takes a known maximum time to execute one step, and every message takes a known maximum time Δ to reach its destination. Δ is a time bound in seconds or milliseconds. The model does not require the clocks of the machines to show the same time. It requires only that the delay is bounded.

With these bounds an execution can be organised in rounds. In each round every process sends its messages, then receives the messages sent in that round, then does local work. A slow process cannot fall behind forever: its step time is bounded. A late message cannot arrive after the round ends: its delay is bounded by Δ. A timeout can therefore be set safely. If a reply does not arrive within the bound, the sender knows that something has failed, not merely that the network is slow.

blocks.where: T_max is the worst-case finish time of a chain; n is the number of processes; w is the maximum work time per process; Δ is the maximum message delay.

blocks.text: This makes the synchronous model easy to reason about. It is used in real-time control, in some hardware buses, and as a teaching model for parallel algorithms. The cost is that the bounds must be true. On the public Internet a router queue can grow without a small fixed limit, so the model often fails. A semi-synchronous model keeps one bound, often on local step time, and drops the other, often on message delay. It is a common middle ground.

Control of a distributed computation means deciding when each process may proceed; the model sets what that control may assume. In the asynchronous model there is no upper bound on message delay and no bound on the time a process takes between steps. A message may take one millisecond or twenty seconds; both are legal. There is no shared clock that can be used to compare events across processes. No timeout can be trusted: a missing reply may mean a crashed process or a very slow one. The consequence is strong. Some problems cannot be solved at all in this model without extra assumptions. Detecting whether a process has crashed is one example; consensus is another. Unit 5 takes up those problems.

Programs still need structure. One common structure is asynchronous execution with synchronous communication. The program is written as rounds: in round r each process sends to a fixed set of neighbours and receives one message from each. The network is asynchronous, but a synchroniser delays the start of round r + 1 until all messages of round r have been delivered. The program then behaves as if it were synchronous, because the logical order of rounds is preserved. This is the basis of synchronisers and of many parallel libraries.

The same idea is called synchronous program order on an asynchronous system. The program's logical order is fixed by sends and receives; real time is not bounded. A receive waits for the matching message, and the code after it runs only when that message has arrived. The order of statements is preserved even when the actual delay is unknown. This is the order that logical clocks in Chapter 4.6 and vector clocks in Chapter 4.7 describe.

examples.question: Four processes P1, P2, P3 and P4 form a chain. Each does 5 ms of local work and then sends one message to the next process. In a synchronous system every message delay is at most 20 ms. (a) Find the maximum time for the chain to finish. (b) Is a 100 ms timeout safe? (c) What changes in the asynchronous model?
steps: Work intervals: 4 processes × 5 ms = 20 ms of local work in total.
Message hops: P1→P2, P2→P3 and P3→P4, so 3 hops. Maximum delay = 3 × 20 ms = 60 ms.
Worst-case finish time = 20 ms + 60 ms = 80 ms.
Timeout slack = 100 ms − 80 ms = 20 ms. Since 20 ms ≥ 0, the timeout is safe in the synchronous model.
In the asynchronous model no delay bound exists. One message may legally take 20 s, so the same 100 ms timeout is a guess, not a guarantee.
examples.answer: The chain finishes within 80 ms, so a 100 ms timeout is safe with 20 ms of slack in the synchronous model; in the asynchronous model it is only a guess.
examples.check:
work_ms = 5
delay_ms = 20
processes = 4
hops = processes - 1
total_ms = processes * work_ms + hops * delay_ms
slack_ms = 100 - total_ms
print(total_ms)
print(slack_ms)

traps: Asynchronous message passing does not mean non-blocking send. It means no bound on delay. A blocking receive can exist in an asynchronous system.
A synchronous model does not require identical physical clocks. It requires bounded step time and bounded message delay.
In an asynchronous system a timeout is not evidence of a crash. A slow process and a crashed process look the same.
An execution is a partial order. Do not draw it as one global time line unless you add a total-order assumption.
Synchronous communication (blocking send and receive) is not the synchronous model. A program can use blocking sends on an asynchronous network.

quiz.a: An event is an internal step, a send or a receive in one process. The local history is the sequence of events of that process.

quiz.q: Why is an execution a partial order and not a single sequence?
quiz.a: Events inside one process are ordered. Events in different processes are ordered only if a message chain connects them. Otherwise either order is possible, so the execution is a partial order.

quiz.q: A chain has 4 processes. Each does 10 ms of work, then sends one message. In a synchronous system each message delay is at most 15 ms. Find the worst-case finish time and the slack against a 100 ms timeout.
quiz.a: Work = 4 × 10 ms = 40 ms. Hops = 3, delay = 3 × 15 ms = 45 ms. Finish = 40 + 45 = 85 ms. Slack = 100 − 85 = 15 ms.

quiz.q: A 100 ms timeout fires in an asynchronous system. Can you conclude that the remote process has crashed? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The asynchronous model has no upper bound on message delay. The reply may still arrive later. A crashed process and a very slow process are indistinguishable by timeout alone.

quiz.q: Name the four failure models listed in this chapter.
What does a synchroniser do in asynchronous execution with synchronous communication?
quiz.a: It delays the start of round r + 1 until all messages of round r have been delivered, so the program keeps a round order even on an asynchronous network.

quiz.q: Why does the synchronous model not need identical physical clocks on all machines?
quiz.a: It assumes a known bound on step time and message delay. Timeouts and rounds use those bounds. No event is ordered by comparing clock readings across machines, so clock equality is not needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real cloud systems sit between the models: RPC deadlines, retries and circuit breakers are guesses about delay, not proofs. Partial synchrony assumes that bounds hold eventually, which is enough for many consensus protocols studied in Unit 5. MPI and many HPC runtimes use synchronisers and barriers to give round-like order on an asynchronous interconnect. Search for partial synchrony, failure detectors, and the asynchronous execution with synchronous communication model.
